body.text: The July 2024 uprising in Bangladesh had many causes, but one ran deepest: for a decade, the main opposition, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), had been shut out of meaningful elections. The uprising promised Bangladeshis that no one would be shut out of politics.

More than two years on, that promise is fraying. A major political party – the Awami League, which was ousted in the July 2024 uprising – is banned, and the ban has become an all-purpose license for arrests and imprisonment. Now it is being turned on workers striking for a wage they can live on. That is bad for democracy, and worse for an economy that cannot afford another crisis of trust.

After the change of government, in October 2024, the Yunus-led interim administration banned the Bangladesh Chhatra League, the Awami League’s student wing, under the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA). On May 12, 2025, it went further, using the newly amended ATA to impose a “temporary” ban on the Awami League itself. The ban covers meetings, publications, and even online speech supporting the party. The Election Commission then suspended its registration.

Under the current law, the ban would remain in effect until party leaders accused of crimes committed while in power are tried. However, the trials could take years, effectively proscribing a party that has existed since before independence. The BNP, which won the 2026 election in which the Awami League was not on the ballot, later codified the ban.

Of particular concern is how the ban is being used. Rights organizations documented at least 8,600 arrests in the “Operation Devil Hunt” campaign alone. Human Rights Watch also found ten murder cases filed against more than 8,400 mostly unnamed people, and hundreds of alleged Awami League supporters held as murder suspects, routinely denied bail. The government allegedly increasingly uses the counterterrorism law against the supporters. Amnesty International said the ban called into question the government’s commitment to freedom of association. Previously, several U.N. experts in a communication reported that the decision to ban the Awami League by executive order “did not follow the ordinary procedure for dissolving political parties under the Political Parties Ordinance 1978.” The lack of judicial oversight of the executive order and the subsequent codification of the law further makes the decision controversial.

The same logic is now being turned on garment workers. Since October 31, hundreds of thousands of workers have walked out across Mirpur, Ashulia, Gazipur, and Narayanganj, demanding a minimum wage of 30,000 Bangladeshi taka ($241). Within a day, police said that the movement had been infiltrated by the Awami League and that many protesters were not genuine garment workers. At the time of writing, police detained 21 people they called Awami League activists and thousands more unidentified individuals under the ATA.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has blamed supporters of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina for the protests, a claim AFP noted he made without evidence, and has also alleged that the unrest is being instigated from across the border.

Given the government’s harsh treatment and the detention of workers under the ATA, many labor leaders have gone into hiding. There is also an allegation of disproportionate force used against laborers during protests. Videos and images circulating on social media appear to show workers being beaten, and police raiding slums to round up protesters; the Awami League label is the justification offered.
The workers rejected the conspiracy theory. Rising food prices, inflation, and energy costs drove them into the streets to survive.

Meanwhile, the economy remains fragile. The World Bank projects 3.4 percent economic growth in both FY26 and FY27—the second-lowest in South Asia, only ahead of Afghanistan. Non-performing loans keep rising; revenue is only 8.3 percent of GDP; about 2.1 million more people have fallen below the poverty margin, and the gap between rich and poor is widening.

The BNP government inherited much of this from the interim administration. Following the formation of the new administration, mob violence and the breakdown of law and order pushed the economy to the brink. Between August 2024 and June 2026, 457 garment and textile factories closed, and more than 240,000 jobs were lost. Most of those who lost their jobs are women. For many, there is no other formal work, and some say employers now screen new hires for union ties. Net foreign direct investment fell to $1.47 billion in FY26, down roughly 13 percent, and no company has listed on the stock market since mid-2024.

Buyers are noticing. A U.S. Fashion Industry Association survey found that the share of U.S. buyers sourcing from Bangladesh fell to about 78 percent from 88 percent a year earlier. Investors and buyers price in political risk, and political exclusion is a political risk.

The current Bangladeshi government’s room to maneuver is further narrowed by a trade deal it did not negotiate. On February 9, 2026, days before the election, the interim administration signed the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States. Under the deal, Bangladesh has now ordered 25 Boeing aircraft this year. On tariffs, 7,132 U.S. products will enter duty-free, up from 441, and almost all US imports are to be duty-free by 2035. For a country that collects only 8.3 percent of GDP in revenue, giving up customs duties while committing to fixed, dollar-denominated purchases is a heavy burden.

The RMG sector is one of the largest contributors to Bangladesh’s foreign reserves, bringing in nearly $39 billion last financial year. Yet, the workers who make these products have always been the most neglected. We have seen this in the rubble of the Rana Plaza, which killed 1,134 people in 2013, and in Tazreen, which killed at least 112 the year before. Today, the entry wage is still the 12,500 taka set in December 2023. Even an experienced sewing operator told Al Jazeera she earns around 15,000 taka a month and sometimes goes hungry.

The government is caught in a real bind. Owners warn that higher wages will raise production costs and push buyers to Vietnam, India or Cambodia. One manufacturer’s leader called the 30,000 taka demand one with “no logical or mathematical basis.”

When political participation is banned, the label becomes a weapon that an authority can use against anyone inconvenient. Today that label is being used against workers asking for a wage that covers rent and rice. Tomorrow it could be students, journalists, or the BNP’s own critics. A democracy that bans its largest rival also loses the ability to tell dissent from sabotage.

It is also bad economics. Buyers value reliability above a few cents of cost. A cheaper supplier becomes more expensive if labor unrest keeps interrupting production. Repression does not create stability; it defers unrest, and the next round of protest is angrier.

Many joined the July uprising on the promise of a country where no one would be excluded from legitimate political participation. Banning a party and branding wage protesters as its agents betrays that promise. Bangladesh cannot rebuild its democracy or its economy by shrinking the space for people to speak.
